title: Admonish the sinner
hookLine: correct gently, as a brother or sister, never with contempt
tomorrow: why were Job's friends at their best before they spoke?

cards: A call-out posted online can go wrong fast: a screenshot, a pile of replies, and the person only digs in deeper. The prophet Nathan had a harder case. He had to tell a king.
So he walked in with a story. A rich man with great flocks has a guest coming, and instead of taking from his own sheep, he takes a poor man's one little ewe lamb, the lamb that slept in his arms.
King David is furious: that man deserves to die! And Nathan says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Thou art the man."

teach.b: So how do you tell someone they're wrong in a way that helps? Nathan's answer: a mirror, not a club.
David had taken another man's wife and arranged her husband's death, and the story let David's own sense of justice do the work. He answered that he had sinned against the Lord.
Jesus gives the order in Matthew: "go, and rebuke him between thee and him alone." Alone first. And the goal: "thou shalt gain thy brother."
Paul adds the tone: set them right "in the spirit of meekness," and watch yourself, because you can be tempted too. That's why the traditional list counts admonishing the sinner as a work of mercy.
It's for the person, never for being right. Now a neighbor who says it too.

The Torah, in the Jewish Publication Society's translation: "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart; thou shalt surely rebuke thy neighbour, and not bear sin because of him." Say it, rather than let it sour inside.
And the Talmud warns that shaming someone in public is like shedding blood. Shared: a hard word, said privately, because you care.

One honest difference: Catholics place this among the spiritual works of mercy, while in Jewish teaching it stands as a commandment of the Torah itself, and the Talmud records sages wondering whether anyone in their generation knew how to give a rebuke well, or to take one.

how: Catholics are taught to correct one another privately first, as in Matthew 18:15, and are encouraged to bring their own faults to the sacrament of confession before correcting anyone else's.

o: correct someone gently, for their sake
warn sinners about hell from a pulpit
report a wrongdoer to the authorities

games.q: how to say the hard word — tap the pairs.
p: a story, then: thou art the man
don't hate your brother in your heart

s: admonishing the sinner means calling people out in public
Jesus says go to them alone first, and the Talmud warns against public shaming.
Nathan told David a story before he named him
David judged the rich man himself, then heard: thou art the man.
Paul says only people without faults may correct others
he says correct gently and watch yourself, because you can be tempted too.

games.q: a friend keeps joking about a classmate's weight. the classmate isn't laughing. you want to say something. which way fits today's texts?
o: later, just you two: that joke lands hard, and you're better than it.
right then, in front of everyone, so the whole group knows it's not okay.
nothing; you've made bad jokes too, so it isn't your place to say.
games.why: alone first, to gain your friend, in a spirit of meekness. Paul's watch yourself is a reason for gentleness, not for silence.

practice: Bring to mind one hard word you've been holding back from someone you care about.
Name what you hope for them, then the thing most likely to make it go wrong, your timing or your tone, then one plan: when and where you'd say it, alone and gently.
Sit with that plan, and if you pray, you can pray for them before you speak.

wordCard.voice: Admonish the sinner. Tell someone a hard truth, privately and gently, for their sake and not to win.

orig.note: Latin: rebuke. the Vulgate's word in Matthew 18:15, between thee and him alone.

carryVoice: Your line: gently. A story, a private word, a mirror instead of a club. Go well.

sources.q: go, and rebuke him between thee and him alone

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 58b (public shaming like shedding blood); Arakhin 16b (who knows how to rebuke, or to accept rebuke)
